description: We are teachers from Kayseri, Turkiye: a mathematics teacher and an English teacher. We love turning real data into stories that students can see, hear and understand. Our team is already formed, and we are not looking for new members.
summary: Erciyes Snow Song is an Earth Information Jukebox that pairs NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) frames with sound generated in real time. As the EIC snow layer over Türkiye plays (2023–2024), the page reads every frame and turns its snow-white area into notes: more snow gives higher notes; with no snow, only wind is heard. A third tab does the same with NASA's global temperature spiral, where more red brings higher notes and a faster beat. At the heart of the jukebox is one mountain: 25 winters (2002–2026) of NASA MODIS snow cover at 25 points on Mount Erciyes, Türkiye, grouped by NASA SRTM elevation into summit, middle slopes and foothills. Each winter is one note, so fewer snow days sound lower. A local legend and a mother's memories of the 1960s frame the data. Snow-covered days fell from 141 to 128 on average (−9%; 95% range −16% to −2%). In an eyes-closed listening test in two classes (47 students), 72% of answers named the trend correctly, against 33% by chance. Climate data is nearly always shown as charts that leave out blind and low-vision learners. The page works in English and Turkish, can read itself aloud, lets anyone make their own data sing, and comes with a free 40-minute lesson kit.
details:
Is the veil melting? Listen before you look.

Erciyes Snow Song pairs NASA Earth Information Center frames with sound generated in real time (EIC tab: every frame of the snow layer over Türkiye becomes a note as it plays), and lets anyone hear how the snow on one mountain has changed. Press play and 25 bars rise one by one while a bağlama plays one note per winter. Choose the bağlama, kanun, piano or flute; listen to the whole mountain, the summit, the middle slopes or the foothills, or to summit and foothills together as a duet. A mountain drawing shows the snow line rise and fall with each winter. A def (Turkish frame drum) beats harder in snowy winters and a wind sound grows when snow is low, so the data reaches the ear twice. Five makams (Uşşak, Hüseyni, Hicaz, Rast, Nihavend) change the mood, never the data.

What it does

  • Jukebox: plays 25 winters (2002–2026) as a melody in makam Uşşak. A studio version adds a bendir drum and a bass line that follows the 5-winter trend.
  • Story: a 60-year timeline: the Ciş Hatun legend, three short recordings of a mother’s memories of the 1960s, two Landsat photos (1 April 1988 and 4 April 2024), and the MODIS record.
  • Eyes-closed listening test: three sounds made from the same 25 values, in real, reversed and shuffled order. Presented as an “Ear Challenge” game: listeners play each sound, say if the second half sounds lower, higher or the same, and earn up to three stars.
  • 40-minute lesson: look, listen, measure, talk; linked to the Türkiye Century Maarif Model outcomes MAT.6.5.1, MAT.6.5.2, MAT.7.6.1, MAT.7.6.2, MAT.6.1.4 (mathematics), FB.8.1.2 (science), SB.5.2.2, SB.5.3.1, SB.6.2.2 (social studies), MÜZ.5.1.6, MÜZ.6.2.1 (music), T.D.5.3 (Turkish) and the grade 6 English theme “Saving Nature”.
  • EIC layer: the first tab of the jukebox (the one that opens first) shows the NASA Earth Information Center snow layer over Türkiye (2023–2024) and sonifies it in real time: while the map plays, the page measures how much of the map area around Türkiye is snow-white in each frame (a 0–100 score, not the real share of land under snow) and turns it into a note. More snow gives a higher note; with no snow the music stops and only wind is heard. We read the map’s pixels on purpose, so that what people see and what they hear match frame by frame; our scientific numbers come from the raw MODIS data, not from this picture.
  • Climate spiral: in the third tab listeners can choose the NASA SVS climate spiral (GISTEMP, 1880–2026). In each frame the page counts the red and orange pixels of the warm rings; more red gives higher notes and a faster beat, so the warming can be heard. The spiral shows the whole planet, not Erciyes; we place them side by side as a question, not as proof: is the mountain’s slow loss of snow days one local trace of global warming? Ground stations and longer records would be needed to say.
  • For teachers (downloads): a one-page lesson plan with answer key and a two-page student worksheet (PDF, English and Turkish), the 25-winter data (CSV), the song and the three test sounds (MP3), the film (MP4), and the analysis code (Python, MIT licence) so anyone can reproduce our numbers or run it for another mountain. Our lesson plan, data, song and test sounds are shared under a CC BY 4.0 licence so any teacher can reuse them.
  • Your own data: a box on the page lets anyone type or paste 5 to 60 numbers (snow days in their town, rainfall, temperature) and hear them on the same instrument. “Every mountain’s snow can sing” already works today for any list of numbers.

How it works

  1. We sampled NASA MODIS/Terra daily snow cover (MOD10A1 v061) at 25 points on Erciyes with NASA AppEEARS.
  2. A day counts as snow when NDSI ≥ 10. Cloudy days are left out: each month’s share of clear days with snow is scaled to the month’s length to estimate its snow-covered days. A winter runs from September to June.
  3. NASA SRTM elevations group the points into summit (6), middle (9) and foothill (10).
  4. Each winter’s snow-covered days choose a note: a 5-winter trend sets the main note, and each winter’s difference from the trend moves it one or two steps.
  5. A plucked-string model synthesises the bağlama in Python. The web jukebox plays its instruments live in the browser, and the EIC layer turns the white pixels over Türkiye in each EIC frame into notes in real time.

What we found

  • Average snow-covered days, first 12 vs last 12 winters: 141 → 128
  • Change over 25 winters: −9% (95% bootstrap range −16% to −2%)
  • Linear trend: about 9 fewer days per decade (linear fit); Mann-Kendall trend test p = 0.04; summit and middle bands also significant, foothill band alone not significant (p = 0.41). These band tests are extra checks: after a Holm correction for three tests none is significant on its own, and we did not correct for autocorrelation, so the overall trend is modest evidence, not proof.
  • Change by band: summit −5% (95% range −10% to 0%), middle −9% (−16% to −2%), foothill −14% (−29% to +3%). On average lower slopes lost more, but the foothill range still includes no change.
  • Least snowy winter: 2024 (102 days); 2026 was snowy (153 days)

The snow is not vanishing; it is slowly thinning, and it varies a lot from year to year.

Who it helps

  • Students hear a trend first, then prove it with a mean and a percentage. In two classes (47 students), 72% of their answers named the trend correctly.
  • Teachers get a free, ready-to-use 40-minute lesson: plan, worksheet and answer key in English and Turkish, linked to curriculum outcomes in mathematics, science, music and social studies. Nothing to install: only the page, speakers and a board. Every student can take part, including those who cannot see a chart. Its listening step was tested in two classes.
  • Blind and low-vision people hear every winter, have the page read aloud, and get the data as a table.
  • Families see an elder’s memory and NASA data meet across sixty years: ask a grandparent what the snow was like when they were young, then listen to the satellite record together, and use the “Make your own data sing” box to hear the numbers of your own town.

Classroom test: 72% correct, chance is 33%. Our school counsellor ran the eyes-closed listening test in two classrooms (47 students). The room was quiet, each student wrote their own answer on paper, and the papers were collected and counted by a helper who did not know which sound was which. Sound A (real order): 35 of 47 correct (74%). Sound B (reversed): 36 of 47 (77%). Sound C (shuffled): 31 of 47 (66%). Overall 102 of 141 answers were correct; with three choices, guessing gives 33%. Both classes gave nearly the same result (73% and 72%). Sound C, “about the same”, was the hardest in both. As a first observation (two people, not a study), a blind colleague at our workplace took the test without seeing anything and answered all three sounds correctly (3 / 3). A blind student answered A and B correctly and C wrong (2 / 3); C was also the hardest sound for the sighted classes. Students’ reactions, reported by our counsellor: some asked, “How did these graphs turn into sound?”; some were surprised that snow data could sound like music; one said, “My ears are very sharp, I can tell everything apart.” All three classes were grade 6. Comparison group: a separate class of 18 students, under the same conditions (answers on their own paper, 15 minutes), saw the same three series as graphs and answered the same question: A 18 of 18, B 17 of 18, C 17 of 18 (52 of 54 answers, 96%). Sighted students read a graph more accurately than they hear the sound, so sound does not replace the graph; it opens a second way in that still lands far above chance (72% vs 33%), and it is the only way in for a student who cannot see the graph. The groups were small and not randomly assigned. Next step: we will run the lesson in four more classes.

Every mountain’s snow can sing. MODIS covers every snowy mountain on Earth. The jukebox already offers instruments of other snowy ranges (quena for the Andes, kalimba for Kilimanjaro, alphorn for the Alps, singing bowl for the Himalaya); they are only tone colours and play Erciyes’s data today, and the same method can give each of those mountains its own song.

What is data and what is music. A table on the page shows which parts of the sound come from the data (pitch, the main note, the drum, the wind) and which are only music (makam, instrument, tempo, the film’s closing cadence).

Related work. Turning data into sound is not new: NASA turns space images into sound (Chandra’s “A Universe of Sound”), and global temperature has been played as music before (Daniel Crawford, “A Song of Our Warming Planet”, 2013). What is new here is one mountain heard from 25 points, a local legend and a mother’s memory set next to the satellite record, and a listening test measured in real classrooms.

Limitations

  • Snow-covered days are not snow depth or water amount.
  • 25 winters is a short record. The foothills lost the most on average, but they vary so much from year to year that their trend alone is not statistically significant.
  • We did not compare with ground weather stations. Cloud filling may undercount snow, because snowy days are often cloudy; this bias works the same way every winter, so it should affect the level more than the trend. Next step: add MODIS/Aqua (MYD10A1) to fill more cloudy days.
  • The test sounds follow a 5-winter moving average, which makes the direction easier to hear: the class test shows that people hear the direction of the change, not its exact size.
  • The closing cadence in the film is a musical ending, not data.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy) for analysis and sound; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio and Web Speech APIs for the page; FFmpeg for the film.

Use of AI and who did what

We used AI as a helper; the idea, the questions, the story, the class work and every decision are ours.

  • Claude (Anthropic): helped write the Python code for the data analysis and the bağlama synthesis, build the web page, edit the film, and draft English text. The team reviewed and checked every result against the data. This is also stated in the code files and in the metadata of every synthesised MP3.
  • ChatGPT and Canva: produced the two illustrations: Erciyes as a bride, and villagers in the 1960s. Both carry a visible “AI-generated illustration” watermark in the film and on the page.
  • No AI-generated data, voices or NASA logos are used. The snow data, the mother’s voice and the classroom results are real.

Who did what. Team: the idea and the question, choosing the legend and the mountain, the mother’s memories and recordings, the lesson design, the worksheet and the classroom tests (47 grade 6 students listening, 18 reading graphs, two blind listeners). The NASA data product and the layout of the 25 points were suggested by AI; the team approved them and downloaded the data. AI (Claude), directed and reviewed by the team: code for the analysis, the music synthesis, the web page and the film editing. AI (ChatGPT, Canva), chosen by the team and watermarked: the two illustrations. English text: drafted with AI, read and checked by our English teacher.

Other sources (not online)

  • Legend: “Ciş Hatun Sandukası”, in Kayseri: Medeniyetlerin Beşiği, Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality, pp. 123–126.
  • Oral history: three recordings of our teammate Şerife’s mother about the 1960s, shared with her written permission.
  • Classroom observation: 47 grade 6 students in two classes guessed from the two Landsat photos how much of the snow was gone: 22 said 80–88%, 6 said 70–79%, 19 said 35–69%. The 25-winter MODIS record shows about 9% fewer snow-covered days: two photos are not a trend.
  • Software: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, FFmpeg, Web Audio API, Web Speech API.
  • Background sources: Immerzeel, W. W. et al., “Importance and vulnerability of the world’s water towers”, Nature 577 (2020); World Health Organization, “Blindness and vision impairment” fact sheet (2026).
  • Fonts (open licences): Bricolage Grotesque, Source Serif 4 and IBM Plex Mono (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License) on the page; DejaVu Sans in the film.
  • Images: two Landsat scenes (NASA/USGS, public domain); NASA SVS visualizations 5480 and 5190 (NASA, public domain). No other third-party images, music or text are used.
